title: Dictator
desc:
The streets of Sevilla were alight with chants and shouts as thousands moved towards the City Hall. Men and women of all walks of life, some even wearing uniforms of the Republican army or factory overalls. They all marched and raised their fists and voices, their voices echoing off the labyrinth of bricks in which they walked.

"Power to the People!" they chanted. "No more Andalucian blood wasted!" they cried.

Alejandro Rojas-Marcos had heard them coming, even despite the large crowd that had assembled before his scaffold at the town hall. He smiled, he had seen this day in his dreams many times in the previous years. He and others who were due to speak watched as the chanting crowds spilled into the square, until eventually the marchers had to wait in the streets. It appeared all of Seville had come.

Alejandro stood up and walked to the prepared podium as the chanting and noise of the crowd died, leaving an eerie stillness. He took a moment to burn the image of Andalusian solidarity before him into his memory before raising his hands.

"Friends, we have all sacrificed. The Republic promised us freedom, but all they gave us was lies. They tried to keep us as servants while we toiled and bled for nothing more than a new dictator."

He paused, a moment of reflection for those whom they had lost. He gestured to the others on the scaffold.

"We have heard you, and we will say no more. If the Republic wishes to ask more of us, it will have to do so with an equal Andalusian state!"

options.name: The applause and cheers deafened the children.

title: If We Could Just Talk
desc:
I`ve seen many people pass by, and despite how I feel my age I still watch them.

Sometimes they are mean, and they curse at me in frustration. Maybe they are thoughtless and leave food, drink or god knows what at my feet, dirtying me. But sometimes I see them happy, embracing a loved one stepping into their world, or a tearful departing as they leave. People are so curious to observe.

They change a lot too. When I was born, the world was much slower. I never really heard other languages, or anyone dressed differently. Maybe it was all the smoke, the steam engines passing through all the time could make it hard to see sometimes. Only occasionally were there cars, and the noise of the crowd deafened me

Later, I remember there was trouble. I remember watching men with guns moving, always moving, through. I remember they began to look so sad after a while, until eventually men with new uniforms arrived, stern faced. I didn't see the old soldiers again.

For a time it felt like before, I saw no one new and few new seemed to come. However the number of cars began to increase, the roar of the crowd being replaced by the roar of nearby traffic. Their styles even began to change, slowly looking far more sleek compared to the old boxes I remembered. Recently, I have even heard many more languages and many strange styles of clothes. Sunglasses and shorts, miniskirts and cameras. The world I was born into seemed so far away.

But now they are gone again. The soldiers came and left again and now yet another new uniform replaces them. Everyday I now wonder, who will use the train next?

options.name: Of humanity, the Sevilla San-Bernardo Train Station watches.

title: A Dream Arrived
desc:
Detractors of Andalucia still lingered in the new state. "This is an artificial state, nothing more than an exaggerated local culture" they bemoaned, their eyes filled with memories of Spain. "There is no Andalusia, only Spain," they would declare to any who would listen.

Often, these proclamations would be on town soapboxes, local government meetings or when deeply drenched with local brews in taverns across the country. These had only increased as news about the Constitutional Convention in Antequera had spread. Some reflected on the change with some amusement, once upon a time it had been the Andalucian nationalists that had occupied such a spot, usually to be carted off by the Guardia Civil for a night in a cell.

As before, people were rising against them in argument. In the taverns it had almost become a popular pastime in the most politically divided areas to watch the drunken sparring over the reality of Andalusia. Vibrant retellings of the 1883 Federal Constitution which had promised recognition of their identity, or the martyrdom of Blas Infante and his preservation of their culture all echoed against the disdain of the Spanish.

Some questioned the reality of some of the stories. To hear of the 1883 Constitution now was to hear the story of a crushed popular liberation which some questioned the exact truth of, but to many it no longer mattered.

They were free, their sons and daughters were no longer dying in unknown fields. From Antequera there was a statement proclaiming the new values of a Andalusian state. They could afford a little bit of the fantastic.

options.name: Andalusia had become both a dream and a reality.

title: Troop the Colors
desc:
The previous weeks had been awash with excitement, but the crescendo was about to come for Luis Urunela.

He'd been approached some time ago to become the provisional Mayor of Seville, a post that carried considerable weight for the activist. His reputation as a unifier had preceded him. In years past he had been a leader in the local left-wing movements, one of the few that had been able to gain the respect of both the most moderate social democrat and the most hardened communist. In the dying days of Iberia when the fate of the Francoists had been clear it was he who had founded the Socialist party of Andalusia, which had been able to unify the once disparate socialist forces. After serving the Republic, as the war had dragged on he had advocated louder for Andalusian separation and many had listened.

He had known Alejandro Rojas-Marcos for years, a partner in the struggle against the Francoists, but he had still felt humbled to be offered such a position.

"Seville in these early days needs someone who could unite them," Alejandro had told him as he asked Luis to lead the new regional Government, "someone who can make it an example for all Andalusia to follow." As far as Luis was concerned, if his skills could aid his comrades then he was happy to be of service.

There was much to do. New elections had to be organized, with zoning and secure counting to be planned. The rescinding of wartime regulations, not to mention a new evaluation of the local economy. At the start of this first session however, Luis allowed himself to simply reflect on the symbol he was witness to. All the Council had assembled to watch as the Spanish Flag which hung from the balcony of the hall was removed. In its place was the green and white of Andalusia.

options.name: A new symbol for the worker.
